options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: D

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a cross-section of a round fleshy fruit: a wide outer pale zone, a dotted wavy boundary inside it, and a central star-shaped core of five chambers holding seeds, with four leader lines labelled P and Q (upper left) and R and S (lower left). Which part each letter points to is the whole question, so it is withheld here. The options are printed as a four-column table under the headings P, Q, R, S, carried here as 'P – ..., Q – ...'. Page idx 2.

rows.stem:
The foetal ejection reflex in human triggers the release of _________ hormone from __________.
Fill in the blanks by choosing right option.

options.label: A
options.text: oxytocin, foetal pituitary

options.label: B
options.text: oxytocin, maternal pituitary

options.label: C
options.text: human chorionic gonadotropin, placenta

options.label: D
options.text: progesterone, corpus luteum

rows.solution: At the end of pregnancy, signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta induce mild uterine contractions, called the **foetal ejection reflex**. This triggers the release of **oxytocin** from the **maternal pituitary**. Oxytocin acts on the uterine muscle and causes stronger contractions, which in turn stimulate further secretion of oxytocin, and the cycle continues until the baby is expelled. So the answer is option (B) oxytocin, maternal pituitary.

rows.stem: A DNA molecule is 160 base pairs long. It has 30% Guanine. How many Adenine bases are present in this DNA molecule ?
rows.solution:
A DNA molecule 160 base pairs long has \(2 \times 160 = 320\) bases. By Chargaff's rule, guanine pairs with cytosine and adenine with thymine, so the amounts of G and C are equal, and so are those of A and T.
- Guanine is 30%, so cytosine is also 30%, and G + C = 60%.
- So A + T = 40%, and adenine alone is 20%.
- Adenine bases = 20% of 320 = \(\frac{20}{100} \times 320 = 64\).

So the answer is option (B) 64.

rows.stem: In Pisum sativum, the flower colour may be violet (V) or white (v). What proportion of the offspring in a cross of 'VV' \(\times\) 'vv' would be expected to be violet ?
rows.solution: Violet (V) is dominant over white (v). The cross 'VV' \(\times\) 'vv' gives gametes V from one parent and v from the other, so every offspring is **Vv**. Since V is dominant, every Vv plant has violet flowers. So the answer is option (D) 100%.

rows.stem:
In a human female, menstrual cycle of 28 days is represented by the diagram given below.
Select the correct statement related with this diagram.

options.label: A
options.text: Primary follicle of ovary matures into Graafian follicle in phase II.

options.label: B
options.text: The hormone secreted in large amounts in phase III is also responsible for maintaining pregnancy in human females.

options.label: C
options.text: Corpus luteum secretes progesterone in phase I, however it degenerates completely in phase III.

options.label: D
options.text: Both (A) and (B).

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a circular diagram of the 28-day cycle: an outer ring of 28 numbered day segments, an arrow captioned 'Cycle starts here' pointing at the boundary between day 28 and day 1, and the inner disc divided by radial lines into three sectors labelled I, II and III. Which days each sector spans decides which phase the statements are about, so the sector boundaries are withheld here. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The diagram divides the 28-day cycle into three phases: phase I is the first few days (the **menstrual phase**), phase II runs up to the middle of the cycle (the **follicular or proliferative phase**, ending with ovulation around day 14), and phase III is the second half (the **luteal or secretory phase**).
- In the follicular phase (II), under FSH and LH, the primary follicles grow into a fully mature **Graafian follicle**. This statement is correct.
- In the luteal phase (III), the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of **progesterone**, which maintains the endometrium. Progesterone is also essential for maintaining pregnancy. This statement is correct.
- The statement about phase I is wrong: the corpus luteum forms after ovulation, in the luteal phase, and it degenerates at the end of that phase when there is no fertilisation, which then starts the menstrual phase.

Both of the first two statements are correct, so the answer is option (D).

rows.stem:
Arrange the following in the correct sequence of their evolution and select the correct option :
(i) Seaweed
(ii) Invertebrates
(iii) Jawless fish

options.label: A
options.text: (i), (ii), (iii)

options.label: B
options.text: (i), (iii), (ii)

options.label: C
options.text: (ii), (iii), (i)

options.label: D
options.text: (ii), (i), (iii)

rows.solution: In the account of evolution given in NCERT, by about **500 mya invertebrates** were formed and active, **jawless fish** probably evolved around **350 mya**, and **seaweeds** and a few plants existed probably around **320 mya**. Following this timeline, the sequence is invertebrates, then jawless fish, then seaweed, that is (ii), (iii), (i). So the answer is option (C) (ii), (iii), (i).

rows.stem: Monascus purpureus is a yeast used commercially in the production of which one of the following ?

options.label: A
options.text: Ethanol

options.label: B
options.text: Streptokinase

options.label: C
options.text: Citric acid

options.label: D
options.text: Statins

rows.solution: The yeast Monascus purpureus is used to produce **statins**, which are commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents. Statins act by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for the synthesis of cholesterol. Ethanol is made with Saccharomyces cerevisiae, streptokinase with Streptococcus, and citric acid with Aspergillus niger. So the answer is option (D) Statins.

rows.stem:
Given below is the restriction site of a restriction endonuclease Pst I and the cleavage sites on a DNA molecule.
5' C – T – G – C – A \(\downarrow\) G 3'
3' G \(\uparrow\) A – C – G – T – C 5'
Choose the option that gives the correct resultant fragments.

options.label: A
options.text: Left: 5' C – T – G / 3' G – A – C – G – T; Right: C – A – G 3' / C 5'

options.label: B
options.text: Left: 5' C – T / 3' G – A – C – G; Right: G – C – A – G 3' / T – C 5'

options.label: C
options.text: Left: 5' C – T – G – C / 3' G – A – C – G; Right: A – G 3' / T – C 5'

options.label: D
options.text: Left: 5' C – T – G – C – A / 3' G; Right: G 3' / A – C – G – T – C 5'

rows.solution:
Pst I recognises the palindromic sequence 5'-CTGCAG-3' and cuts each strand between A and G, as the arrows show:
- top strand 5'-CTGCA \(\downarrow\) G-3' gives 5'-CTGCA and G-3';
- bottom strand 3'-G \(\uparrow\) ACGTC-5' gives 3'-G and ACGTC-5'.

The left fragment is therefore 5'-CTGCA-3' paired with only a 3'-G on the bottom strand, and the right fragment is G-3' on top with ACGTC-5' below. The cut is staggered, so each fragment carries a single-stranded overhang, a **sticky end**. So the answer is option (D), the fragments 5' C – T – G – C – A / 3' G and G 3' / A – C – G – T – C 5'.

rows.stem: Choose a correct option that shows an interaction in which one species benefits while the other is neither harmed nor benefitted.

options.label: A
options.text: Mycorrhizal associations between fungi and roots of higher plants

options.label: B
options.text: Sea anemone and clownfish

options.label: C
options.text: Abingdon tortoises and goats in the Galapagos Island

options.label: D
options.text: Cuscuta on hedge plants

rows.solution: An interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited is **commensalism**. The clownfish lives among the stinging tentacles of the sea anemone and gets protection from predators, which stay away from the stinging tentacles, while the sea anemone does not appear to gain anything. Mycorrhiza is mutualism, the Abingdon tortoise and the goats is competition, and Cuscuta on hedge plants is parasitism. So the answer is option (B) Sea anemone and clownfish.

rows.stem: Transgenic animals have their genetic material manipulated. Select the correct option in reference to transgenic animals.

options.label: A
options.text: Foreign DNA and RNA are present in their cells.

options.label: B
options.text: Foreign RNA is present in all of their cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Foreign DNA is present in all of its cells.

options.label: D
options.text: Foreign RNA is present in some of its cells.

rows.solution: Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are called **transgenic animals**. The foreign gene is introduced into the early embryo, so it is a part of the DNA and is carried into **all the cells** of the animal that develops. The foreign material is DNA, not RNA. So the answer is option (C) Foreign DNA is present in all of its cells.

rows.stem: Select the odd option in the context of convergent evolution.

options.label: A
options.text: Eyes of Octopus and Mammals

options.label: B
options.text: Flippers of Penguins and Dolphins

options.label: C
options.text: Flying Squirrel and Flying Phalanger

options.label: D
options.text: Thorns of Bougainvillea and Tendrils of Cucurbita

rows.solution: Convergent evolution produces **analogous** structures: different structures, with different origins, that evolve to perform the same function. The eyes of the octopus and of mammals, the flippers of penguins and dolphins, and the flying squirrel and the flying phalanger (a placental mammal and a marsupial that look alike) are all examples of it. The thorn of Bougainvillea and the tendril of Cucurbita are **homologous** organs: both are modified stems, with the same origin but different functions, which is divergent evolution. So the answer is option (D) Thorns of Bougainvillea and Tendrils of Cucurbita.

rows.stem: Which of the following fish led to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in Lake Victoria of East Africa ?

options.label: A
options.text: Catla Catla

options.label: B
options.text: Dogfish

options.label: C
options.text: Nile Perch

options.label: D
options.text: African Catfish

rows.solution: Alien species invasions are one of the causes of loss of biodiversity. When the **Nile perch** was introduced into Lake Victoria in East Africa, it led eventually to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake. So the answer is option (C) Nile Perch.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula.
Reason (R) : The morula continues to divide and transform into trophoblast.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: the embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a **morula**. The Reason is false: the morula continues to divide and transforms into the **blastocyst**. The trophoblast is only the outer layer of the blastocyst, the layer that attaches to the endometrium, while the inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Repetitive sequences make up a very large portion of human genome.
Reason (R) : Repetitive sequences do not have direct coding functions in the genome.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: one of the salient features of the human genome is that **repetitive sequences make up a very large portion** of it. The Reason is also true: repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA repeated many times, and they are thought to have **no direct coding functions**, though they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution. But the lack of a coding function does not explain why such sequences make up so much of the genome. So both statements are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Trichoderma species are free living fungi that are very common in the root ecosystems.
Reason (R) : They are effective bio-control agents of several plant pathogens.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The Assertion is true: Trichoderma species are free-living fungi that are very common in root ecosystems. The Reason is also true: they are effective **biocontrol agents** of several plant pathogens. But being biocontrol agents does not explain why they are free-living and common in the root ecosystem; the two statements are separate facts about the fungus. So both statements are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.subtopic: Isolation, Cutting and Amplification of DNA
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The use of chitinase enzyme is necessary for the separation of DNA from yeast cells but not in the case of Spirogyra.
Reason (R) : Fungal cell wall is made up of fungal chitin.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: To isolate DNA, the cell must be broken open by treating it with enzymes that break down its wall. Yeast is a fungus and its cell wall is made of **chitin**, so **chitinase** is needed for it. Spirogyra is an alga with a **cellulose** cell wall, so it needs cellulase instead, not chitinase. The Assertion is true, and the Reason (the fungal cell wall is made of chitin) is true and is exactly why chitinase is needed for yeast. So both statements are true and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (A).

rows.stem:
Mention the functions of each of the following :
(i) Tassels of Corn Cob
(ii) Scutellum
rows.solution:
CBSE awarded the mark for part (i) to every student who attempted it.

(i) **Tassels of the corn cob**: NCERT describes the tassels seen on the corn cob as the **stigma and style**, which wave in the wind to **trap pollen grains**. Maize is wind-pollinated, and these long feathery stigmas help catch the pollen carried in the air. (Botanically, these hairs on the cob are called the silk, and the tassel at the top of a maize plant is its male inflorescence.)

(ii) **Scutellum**: it is the single large, shield-shaped cotyledon of the grass family (for example maize). It lies against the endosperm and **provides nourishment to the embryo** by absorbing the food stored in the endosperm.

rows.stem: Farmers prefer apomictic seeds over hybrid seeds. Give any two reasons.
rows.solution:
Any two reasons:
- Production of hybrid seed is **very costly**, and the farmer must buy fresh hybrid seed every year, because the progeny of hybrid seeds segregate and do not keep the hybrid characters.
- If the hybrids are made into apomicts, there is **no segregation of characters** in the hybrid progeny, so the farmer can keep using the seeds to raise new crops year after year.
- Using apomictic seeds is therefore **cost effective** for the farmer.

rows.stem: Define the term 'amniocentesis'. Why has the government imposed a statutory ban in spite of its importance in the medical field ?
rows.solution:
**Amniocentesis** is a foetal sex determination test based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing embryo: some of the foetal cells present in the amniotic fluid are analysed for certain genetic disorders.

Because it reveals the sex of the foetus, it is **misused** to determine the sex of the unborn child, and this is followed by the abortion of normal female foetuses (female foeticide). The government imposed a statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination to legally check this increasing menace of female foeticide.

rows.stem: Name the lymphoid organ that acts as a large reservoir of erythrocytes. Explain its role as a lymphoid organ.
rows.solution:
The **spleen** is the lymphoid organ that acts as a large reservoir of erythrocytes.

As a lymphoid organ, the spleen is a large bean-shaped organ that mainly contains **lymphocytes and phagocytes**. It acts as a **filter of the blood** by trapping blood-borne microorganisms, which are then destroyed.

rows.stem: Suggest how a virus-free healthy plant can be obtained from a diseased sugarcane plant.
rows.solution: A virus-free plant is obtained by **meristem culture**. Even when a plant is infected with a virus, its **meristem** (the apical and axillary meristem) is free of the virus. So the meristem is removed from the diseased sugarcane plant and grown **in vitro** by tissue culture on a nutrient medium, and the plants raised from it are virus-free.

rows.stem: In order to force bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA, they must be made competent. Explain how it can be achieved.
Ecological pyramids are widely accepted but they still have some limitations. Write any two limitations.
rows.solution:
Any two limitations of ecological pyramids:
- They do not take into account the same species belonging to **two or more trophic levels**.
- They assume a **simple food chain**, something that almost never exists in nature.
- They do not accommodate a **food web**.
- **Saprophytes** are not given any place in ecological pyramids, even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.

rows.stem: List any three outbreeding devices that flowering plants have developed for cross-pollination and explain how they help to encourage cross-pollination.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: it says that unisexual flowers leave no chance of self-pollination. That holds when the male and female flowers are on different plants (dioecy). On a monoecious plant such as castor or maize, unisexual flowers prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy, which is genetically still self-pollination.]

Continued self-pollination results in inbreeding depression, so flowering plants have developed several devices to discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination. Any three:
- **Pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised**: either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive, or the stigma becomes receptive much before the pollen is released, so a flower cannot pollinate itself.
- **Anther and stigma are placed at different positions**, so that the pollen cannot come in contact with the stigma of the same flower.
- **Self-incompatibility**: a genetic mechanism that prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or from other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules, by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
- **Production of unisexual flowers**: if male and female flowers are borne on different plants (dioecy, as in papaya), both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented, so only cross-pollination is possible.

rows.stem: Draw a labelled diagram of a 'replicating fork' showing the polarity. Why does DNA replication occur within such 'fork' ?

Study the given chart showing evolution of plants. Answer the following questions :
(a) Identify the plant which acts as an immediate ancestor of both ferns and conifers.
(b) Name the nearest ancestors of flowering plants.
(c) Name the most primitive group of plants.
(d) Psilophyton provides common ancestry to which classes ?
(e) Name the common ancestor of psilophyton and seed ferns.
(f) Name the common ancestor of mosses and tracheophytes.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: a branching chart of eight boxes: Moss, Ferns, Conifers and Flowering plants along the top, Seed ferns below Flowering plants, and Psilophyton, Tracheophyte ancestors and Chlorophyte ancestors stacked in the lower middle, joined by upward arrows. Which box each arrow leaves and reaches answers every part, so the connections are withheld here. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
Reading the chart from the bottom upwards:
(a) **Psilophyton** is the immediate ancestor of both ferns and conifers.
(b) **Seed ferns** are the nearest ancestors of flowering plants.
(c) **Chlorophyte ancestors** are the most primitive group of plants, at the base of the chart.
(d) Psilophyton provides common ancestry to **ferns, conifers and seed ferns**.
(e) The common ancestor of Psilophyton and seed ferns is the **tracheophyte ancestors**.
(f) The common ancestor of mosses and tracheophytes is the **chlorophyte ancestors**.

rows.stem:
Mention a product of human welfare obtained with the help of each one of the following :
(a) Saccharomyces cerevisiae
(b) Propionibacterium shermanni
(c) Aspergillus niger
(d) Trichoderma polysporum
(e) Acetobacter aceti
(f) Streptococcus
rows.solution:
(a) Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's or baker's yeast): **bread** and other bakery products, and **ethanol** or beverages.
(b) Propionibacterium shermanni: **Swiss cheese**, whose large holes are due to the large amount of carbon dioxide this bacterium produces.
(c) Aspergillus niger: **citric acid**.
(d) Trichoderma polysporum: **cyclosporin A**, used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients.
(e) Acetobacter aceti: **acetic acid**.
(f) Streptococcus: **streptokinase**, used as a clot buster for removing clots from the blood vessels of patients who have had a heart attack.

rows.stem: Transgenic animals are produced by man. Explain any three ways in which such animals can be beneficial to humans.
rows.solution:
Any three ways in which transgenic animals benefit humans:
- **Normal physiology and development**: transgenic animals are made to study how genes are regulated and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development, for example complex factors involved in growth such as insulin-like growth factor.
- **Study of disease**: many transgenic animals are designed to increase our understanding of how genes contribute to the development of disease, so that new treatments can be investigated. Transgenic models exist for human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's.
- **Biological products**: transgenic animals that produce useful biological products are created by introducing the portion of DNA that codes for a particular product, such as human protein (\(\alpha\)-1-antitrypsin) used to treat emphysema. In 1997 the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre) containing human alpha-lactalbumin, nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk.
- **Vaccine safety**: transgenic mice are being developed for use in testing the safety of vaccines, such as the polio vaccine, before they are used on humans. If successful and found reliable, they could replace the use of monkeys to test the safety of batches of the vaccine.
- **Chemical safety testing (toxicity testing)**: transgenic animals are made to carry genes that make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals. They are exposed to the toxic substances and the effects studied, giving results in less time.

rows.stem: Explain Gause's 'Competitive Exclusion Principle' with the help of a suitable example.
rows.solution:
**Gause's 'Competitive Exclusion Principle'** states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely, and the **competitively inferior one will be eliminated** eventually. This holds when the resources are limited; the stronger competitor dominates and drives the weaker one out.

Example (any one):
- In the Galapagos Islands, the **Abingdon tortoise** became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats.
- In some shallow South American lakes, visiting **flamingoes and resident fishes** compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake.
- On the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area and excludes the smaller barnacle Chthamalus from that zone.

rows.subtopic: Species Numbers and Patterns of Biodiversity
rows.stem: Explain the level of biodiversity at genetic, species and ecological levels with the help of one example each.
rows.solution:
- **Genetic diversity**: a single species can show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. Example: the medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical (reserpine) it produces; India also has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
- **Species diversity**: the diversity at the species level, that is the number of different species in a region. Example: the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.
- **Ecological diversity**: the diversity at the ecosystem level. Example: India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has a greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

rows.stem: Why is the strand of DNA with 3' \(\longrightarrow\) 5' polarity transcribed and not the other strand of 5' \(\longrightarrow\) 3' polarity ?
rows.context: The process of copying genetic information from template strand of DNA into RNA is called transcription. It is mediated by RNA polymerase. Transcription takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. In transcription, only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.
rows.solution: The DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses polymerisation in **only one direction, 5' to 3'**. To build an RNA in the 5' to 3' direction, it must read the template in the opposite direction, so the strand with **3' to 5' polarity** acts as the template. The other strand, with 5' to 3' polarity, has the same sequence as the RNA (with thymine in place of uracil) and is called the coding strand.

rows.stem: Why is hnRNA required to undergo splicing ?
rows.context: The process of copying genetic information from template strand of DNA into RNA is called transcription. It is mediated by RNA polymerase. Transcription takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. In transcription, only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.
rows.solution: The primary transcript in eukaryotes, the hnRNA, contains both the coding sequences (**exons**) and the non-coding sequences (**introns**), because eukaryotic genes are split genes. The introns are not functional, so the hnRNA undergoes **splicing**, in which the introns are removed and the exons are joined in a defined order.

rows.stem: Mention the two additional processes which hnRNA needs to undergo after splicing to become functional.
rows.context: The process of copying genetic information from template strand of DNA into RNA is called transcription. It is mediated by RNA polymerase. Transcription takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. In transcription, only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: it says the adenylate residues are added at the 3' end "in a template strand". The poly A tail is added at the 3' end of the hnRNA in a template-independent manner; no DNA template is used for it.]

The two additional processes are:
- **Capping**: an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, is added to the **5' end** of the hnRNA.
- **Tailing**: adenylate residues (200-300) are added at the **3' end** in a template-independent manner, forming the poly A tail.

The fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, is transported out of the nucleus for translation.

rows.stem: Why is only one strand of the DNA transcribed ? Give two reasons.
rows.context: The process of copying genetic information from template strand of DNA into RNA is called transcription. It is mediated by RNA polymerase. Transcription takes place in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. In transcription, only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.
rows.solution:
Only one strand of DNA is transcribed because if both strands acted as templates:
- they would code for RNA molecules with **different sequences**. If they in turn coded for proteins, the sequence of amino acids in the proteins would be different, so one segment of DNA would code for two different proteins, and this would complicate the genetic information transfer machinery.
- the two RNA molecules, being **complementary** to each other if produced simultaneously, would form a **double-stranded RNA**, which would prevent the RNA from being translated into protein, and the exercise of transcription would become futile.

rows.stem: Why are plasmids and bacteriophages used as cloning vectors ?
rows.context: We know that plasmids and bacteriophages are the most commonly used vectors in biotechnology experiments. If we can link an alien piece of DNA to the plasmid DNA, the alien DNA can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid. Engineered vectors are used these days. Study the diagram of the E. coli cloning vector pBR322 and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE: the case study's map of pBR322: a double ring divided into segments, Cla I and Hind III printed at the top, six letters A, B, C, D, E and F on leader lines round the outside, two letters G and H inside the ring, and ori and rop written inside the ring at the bottom. This sub-part is answerable without it. Page idx 18.
rows.solution: Plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to **replicate within bacterial cells independently** of the control of the chromosomal DNA. Bacteriophages, because of their high number per cell, have very high copy numbers of their genome within the bacterial cells, and some plasmids have only one or two copies per cell while others have 15-100 copies. If an alien piece of DNA is **linked** to them, it can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid or bacteriophage. This is why they are used as cloning vectors.

rows.stem:
Identify :
(I) The gene in the cloning vector that controls the copy number of the vector.
(II) The restriction site – C in the 'rop' gene.
rows.context: We know that plasmids and bacteriophages are the most commonly used vectors in biotechnology experiments. If we can link an alien piece of DNA to the plasmid DNA, the alien DNA can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid. Engineered vectors are used these days. Study the diagram of the E. coli cloning vector pBR322 and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's map of pBR322: a double ring divided into segments, Cla I and Hind III printed at the top, six letters A, B, C, D, E and F on leader lines round the outside, two letters G and H inside the ring, and ori and rop written inside the ring at the bottom. Which site the letter C marks is read off the drawing, so the placement of the lettered sites is withheld here. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(I) **ori**: the sequence from where replication starts. Any piece of DNA linked to it can be made to replicate within the host cells, and it is also responsible for **controlling the copy number** of the linked DNA.

(II) The restriction site C, lying in the rop region, is **Pvu II**.

rows.stem: Identify and name two selectable markers shown in the diagram.
rows.context: We know that plasmids and bacteriophages are the most commonly used vectors in biotechnology experiments. If we can link an alien piece of DNA to the plasmid DNA, the alien DNA can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid. Engineered vectors are used these days. Study the diagram of the E. coli cloning vector pBR322 and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's map of pBR322: a double ring divided into segments, Cla I and Hind III printed at the top, six letters A, B, C, D, E and F on leader lines round the outside, two letters G and H inside the ring, and ori and rop written inside the ring at the bottom. Which gene region G and H mark is read off the drawing, so their placement is withheld here. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The two selectable markers shown are the antibiotic resistance genes:
- **G: ampR**, the ampicillin resistance gene;
- **H: tetR**, the tetracycline resistance gene.

Selectable markers help in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.

rows.stem: Name the two restriction sites each in the two genes you have identified as selectable markers.
rows.context: We know that plasmids and bacteriophages are the most commonly used vectors in biotechnology experiments. If we can link an alien piece of DNA to the plasmid DNA, the alien DNA can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid. Engineered vectors are used these days. Study the diagram of the E. coli cloning vector pBR322 and answer the questions that follow :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED: the case study's map of pBR322: a double ring divided into segments, Cla I and Hind III printed at the top, six letters A, B, C, D, E and F on leader lines round the outside, two letters G and H inside the ring, and ori and rop written inside the ring at the bottom. The two marker genes this part builds on are the regions lettered on the drawing, so their placement is withheld here. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The restriction sites in the two selectable marker genes of pBR322:
- in the ampicillin resistance gene (ampR): **Pvu I** and **Pst I**;
- in the tetracycline resistance gene (tetR): **BamH I** and **Sal I**.

When foreign DNA is ligated at one of these sites, the antibiotic resistance gene is inactivated (insertional inactivation), which is how the recombinants are told apart from the non-recombinants.

rows.stem: Briefly explain the events of fertilisation and implantation in an adult human female.
rows.solution:
**Fertilisation**
- During copulation, semen is released by the penis into the vagina. The motile sperms swim through the cervix, enter the uterus and finally reach the junction of the isthmus and ampulla (the **ampullary-isthmic junction**) of the fallopian tube.
- The ovum released by the ovary is also transported to the ampullary region, where fertilisation takes place. Fertilisation can happen only if the ovum and sperms are transported simultaneously to this region.
- The **secretions of the acrosome** help the sperm to enter the cytoplasm of the ovum through the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane.
- When a sperm comes in contact with the zona pellucida layer of the ovum, it induces **changes in the membrane that block the entry of additional sperms**, so only one sperm fertilises an ovum.
- The entry of the sperm induces the completion of the **meiotic division of the secondary oocyte**, forming a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid).
- The haploid nucleus of the sperm and that of the ovum fuse to form a **diploid zygote**.

**Implantation**
- The zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage) as it moves through the isthmus towards the uterus, forming the **morula** (8-16 blastomeres), which develops into the **blastocyst**. The blastomeres of the blastocyst are arranged into an outer layer, the **trophoblast**, and an inner group of cells, the inner cell mass.
- The **trophoblast layer gets attached to the endometrium**.
- The **uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst**, so the blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium of the uterus. This is called implantation, and it leads to pregnancy.

rows.stem:
(i) Arrange the following hormones in sequence of their secretion in a pregnant woman :
hCG; LH; FSH; Relaxin.
(ii) Mention the source and the functions of the above mentioned hormones.
rows.solution:
(i) In sequence of secretion: **FSH; LH; hCG; Relaxin**.

(ii) Source and functions:
- **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone): secreted by the **anterior pituitary**. It stimulates follicular development and the secretion of estrogens by the growing follicles.
- **LH** (luteinising hormone): secreted by the **anterior pituitary**. Its rapid rise in the middle of the cycle (the LH surge) induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle and the release of the ovum (**ovulation**), and it also stimulates the formation of the corpus luteum.
- **hCG** (human chorionic gonadotropin): secreted by the **placenta**. It is needed for supporting foetal growth, metabolic changes in the mother and the **maintenance of pregnancy**.
- **Relaxin**: secreted by the **ovary** in the later phase of pregnancy. It helps to **facilitate parturition** (childbirth).

rows.stem: Work out separate monohybrid crosses up to \(\text{F}_2\) generation between two pea plants and two Antirrhinum plants, both having contrasting traits with respect to the colour of the flower. Comment on the patterns of inheritance in the crosses carried out in such two cases.
rows.solution:
**Pea plants (flower colour): dominance**

Violet (V) is dominant over white (v).
- Parents: VV (violet) \(\times\) vv (white)
- Gametes: V and v
- \(\text{F}_1\): Vv, all violet
- \(\text{F}_1\) selfed: Vv \(\times\) Vv, gametes V, v from each parent

\(\text{F}_2\):

| Gametes | V | v |
|---|---|---|
| V | VV (violet) | Vv (violet) |
| v | Vv (violet) | vv (white) |

Phenotypic ratio violet : white = 3 : 1; genotypic ratio 1 VV : 2 Vv : 1 vv. Only violet appears in \(\text{F}_1\) although its genotype is Vv, and white reappears in \(\text{F}_2\). This is the case of **dominance**: the violet allele is dominant and the white allele recessive.

**Antirrhinum (snapdragon, flower colour): incomplete dominance**

- Parents: RR (red) \(\times\) rr (white)
- Gametes: R and r
- \(\text{F}_1\): Rr, all **pink**
- \(\text{F}_1\) selfed: Rr \(\times\) Rr, gametes R, r from each parent

\(\text{F}_2\):

| Gametes | R | r |
|---|---|---|
| R | RR (red) | Rr (pink) |
| r | Rr (pink) | rr (white) |

Phenotypic ratio red : pink : white = 1 : 2 : 1, the same as the genotypic ratio 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr. Here the \(\text{F}_1\) has a phenotype (pink) that does not resemble either parent and is in between the two, because R is not completely dominant over r. This is the case of **incomplete dominance**.

So the pea cross gives a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio that differs from its 1 : 2 : 1 genotypic ratio, while in Antirrhinum the phenotypic and genotypic ratios are the same, 1 : 2 : 1.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) How does a chromosomal disorder differ from a Mendelian disorder ? Write one example for each.
(ii) Name the phenomenon that leads to situations like 'XO' abnormality in humans. Also name this genetic disorder. How are individuals with an XO chromosomal abnormality affected ? Write its symptoms as well as karyotype.
rows.solution:
(i) Differences:

| Mendelian disorder | Chromosomal disorder |
|---|---|
| Caused by alteration or mutation in a **single gene** | Caused by the absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of **one or more chromosomes** |
| Transmitted to the offspring along the Mendelian principles of inheritance, so its pattern can be traced in a pedigree | Does not follow the Mendelian pattern of inheritance |

Examples: Mendelian disorder, **haemophilia** (or cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia); chromosomal disorder, **Down's syndrome** (or Turner's syndrome, Klinefelter's syndrome).

(ii) Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division results in the gain or loss of a chromosome, called **aneuploidy**; the loss of one X chromosome here is a monosomy. The disorder is **Turner's syndrome**.

Such individuals are females with the following symptoms (any three):
- they are **sterile**, as the ovaries are rudimentary;
- they **lack the other secondary sexual characters**;
- they are of **short stature**, with underdeveloped feminine characters.

Karyotype: **44 + XO**, a total of 45 chromosomes.

rows.stem:
(i) Draw the structure of an antibody molecule and label any four of its parts.
(ii) Differentiate between active and passive immunity. Write any three differences.
rows.solution:
(i) The antibody molecule is drawn as a **Y-shaped** structure with four peptide chains, two small **light chains** and two longer **heavy chains**, hence it is represented as \(\text{H}_2\text{L}_2\). The two heavy chains form the stem of the Y and run up both arms, and a light chain lies along the outer side of each arm. The chains are held together by **disulphide bonds**. The tips of the two arms are the **antigen binding sites**, with the N ends of the chains there and the C ends at the base of the stem. Any four labels: antigen binding site, light chain, heavy chain, disulphide bonds.

(ii) Any three differences:

| Active immunity | Passive immunity |
|---|---|
| The host's own body produces antibodies in response to an antigen | Ready-made antibodies are given directly to the body for protection |
| It is slow and takes time to give its full effective response | It gives a quick response |
| It lasts for a longer period | It lasts for a shorter period |
| Memory cells are formed | Memory cells are not formed |

rows.stem:
(i) (I) Write the scientific names of the two species of filarial worms causing filariasis.
(II) How do they affect the body of infected persons ?
(III) How does the disease spread ?
(ii) Mention the source and the role of the following in providing defence against infection in the human body :
(I) Histamine
(II) Interferons
rows.solution:
(i) (I) Filariasis is caused by the filarial worms **Wuchereria bancrofti** and **Wuchereria malayi**.

(II) The filarial worms live in the **lymphatic vessels** (usually of the lower limbs) for many years and cause a slowly developing **chronic inflammation** of the organs in which they live. The disease is called elephantiasis or filariasis, and it causes **swelling of the lower limbs**; the genital organs are also often affected, resulting in gross deformities.

(III) The pathogens are transmitted to a healthy person through the **bite of the female mosquito vectors**.

(ii) (I) **Histamine**: it is released by the **mast cells** (and basophils). It causes the dilation of blood vessels and increased capillary permeability, producing the inflammatory and **allergic** response; the inflammation brings the defensive cells to the site of an infection.

(II) **Interferons**: they are secreted by **virus-infected cells**. They act as a cytokine barrier and **protect the non-infected cells** of the body from further viral infection.
